metadata.title: New technology, new role of parents: How parents' beliefs and behavior affect students’ digital media self-efficacy

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a multi-cohort longitudinal school initiative in Baden-Württemberg (Germany) with 56 classes in 28 schools, and it matches parent and student questionnaires via identification codes. The analysis focuses on mediation models with self-report measures of parents’ task values and behaviors (modeling/provision) and students’ digital media self-efficacy; the paper does not describe the use of complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the dependent variable is a Likert-scale self-efficacy scale adapted from PISA items (not an ILSA achievement score with plausible values), PV-based weighting is not relevant. The only explicit weighting described is internal to the construction of parent screen-time variables (averaging weekday/weekend time across owned devices), not survey-weighted population inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is students’ digital media self-efficacy measured with a Likert-scale scale adapted from PISA items, rather than a cognitive achievement score for which ICILS/PISA typically generate plausible values. The paper also does not report any PV-based scaling or PV benchmarks for the outcome, so PV handling cannot be mapped to standard ILSA PV procedures.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample consists of 1,206 parent questionnaires that could be matched to student questionnaires from both seventh-grade cohorts (February 2018 and February 2019). Parent or student questionnaires that could not be matched using the identification code were excluded. The analysis uses student data collected at the first measurement point before students in tablet classes received tablets. Parents’ responses were aggregated when two parents responded for the same student (n=236), using intra-class correlation to justify aggregation. The paper does not report additional exclusions by missingness beyond the stated missing-data handling in Mplus.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 the study leveraged Intrinsic value (digital media), Utility value (digital media), Attainment value (digital media) to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This study does not use machine learning prediction on ICILS/PISA achievement scores; instead, it tests mediation relationships in a school-based longitudinal design in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Students’ digital media self-efficacy was measured at the first measurement point (before tablet provision) using a 7-item Likert scale adapted from PISA 2015, while parents reported task values (intrinsic, utility, attainment, emotional cost, opportunity cost) and two behavior pathways: modeling (average daily screen time on phone/tablet/computer) and provision (whether the child has each device and the age at which it was provided). The mediation models were estimated in Mplus with missing data handled via maximum likelihood estimation, and indirect effects were assessed using 10,000 bootstrap samples. Across five parallel mediation models, the only indirect effect consistently different from zero was through the age at which parents provided their child with a smart phone; other mediators (time spent on devices and provision ages for tablet/computer) did not robustly mediate the belief–self-efficacy links. The paper reports standardized path estimates and 95% confidence intervals (Table 5) rather than ML metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC). Limitations include the inability to infer causality due to the cross-sectional measurement of beliefs and self-efficacy at the same time point and potential measurement bias from self-reports. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ILSA program/cycle and ML outputs because the paper is an empirical mediation study using a local German school initiative rather than an ICILS/PISA micro-data analysis with ML prediction. Although the self-efficacy scale is adapted from PISA items and the introduction references ICILS 2018 results, the methods section describes a custom parent questionnaire and mediation modeling (Mplus) rather than ML training/evaluation. Consequently, there are no ML techniques to extract and no ILSA PV-handling or country-level ICILS/PISA sampling details to populate.
